title: Fournier Gangrene: Recognition, Resuscitation and Emergency Debridement

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with suspected Fournier gangrene (necrotising soft-tissue infection of the perineum and genitals) in the ED: recognition, Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotising Fasciitis (LRINEC) limits, resuscitation, surgery within 12 hours, antibiotics, glucose control and repeat debridement. Uses the World Society of Emergency Surgery / Surgical Infection Society Europe (WSES/SIS-E) 2018 consensus, IDSA 2014 and a StatPearls review for doses.
findings: Rebuilt from the thin 21 Oct 2026 version: frequencies of signs, LRINEC with its limits, the 12-hour source-control standard, re-look at 24–36 hours, two antibiotic branches including clindamycin toxin suppression, glucose targets and six management steps added.
Antibiotic doses come from a labelled review (StatPearls) because the opened guidelines name drugs without doses.
All thresholds trace to sources opened on 22 Oct 2026.

pathophysiology.summary: Fournier gangrene is a necrotising soft-tissue infection of the scrotum and penis or vulva (VUMC protocol, Definition). It is usually polymicrobial — group A streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa; clostridia produce gas (StatPearls, Section Etiology). Infection can spread about 2.5 cm per hour along fascial planes (StatPearls, Section Pathophysiology). Diabetes is present in 20–70% and chronic alcohol misuse in 25–50% (StatPearls, Section Etiology).
keyMechanisms: Polymicrobial fascial infection of the perineum and genitals (StatPearls, Section Etiology).
Spread up to about 2.5 cm per hour (StatPearls, Section Pathophysiology).
Tissue necrosis beyond visible skin change; skin necrosis and bullae are late (WSES/SIS-E 2018, Section Clinical signs).
Toxin-mediated shock with streptococci; clindamycin suppresses toxin (IDSA 2014, Section VIII).

symptoms: Severe perineal or genital pain out of proportion to the findings (WSES/SIS-E 2018, Recommendation on clinical signs).
Prodrome of 2–7 days; median delay to hospital about 5 days (StatPearls, Section History and Physical).
Fever in 41% (StatPearls, Section History and Physical).
Malaise, vomiting, confusion as sepsis develops (WSES/SIS-E 2018, Section Clinical signs).
physicalSigns: Scrotal swelling in 79% (StatPearls, Section History and Physical).
Tachycardia in 61%; purulent drainage in 60% (StatPearls, Section History and Physical).
Crepitus in 54% (StatPearls, Section History and Physical).
Oedema beyond the erythema, bullae or skin necrosis (WSES/SIS-E 2018, Section Clinical signs).
redFlags: Hypotension or shock (WSES/SIS-E 2018, Section Clinical signs).
Rapid spread of erythema or swelling (StatPearls, Section Pathophysiology).
Crepitus or skin necrosis (WSES/SIS-E 2018, Section Clinical signs).
Up to 75% are first misdiagnosed — reassess any perineal infection with severe pain (StatPearls, Section History and Physical).
precipitants: Colorectal, urogenital or skin source (StatPearls, Section Etiology).
No cause found in about 25% (StatPearls, Section Etiology).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Superficial erythema without pain out of proportion, crepitus or systemic toxicity (WSES/SIS-E 2018, Section Clinical signs).
Localised fluctuant collection; spreading pain, crepitus or shock indicate necrotising infection.
Testicular pain without spreading perineal skin involvement.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Pain out of proportion, oedema beyond erythema and fever suggest necrotising infection; treat a rapidly progressing infection as necrotising (WSES/SIS-E 2018, Recommendation, grade 1C).

C-reactive protein (CRP) above 150 mg/L, white cells above 15 ×10⁹/L, haemoglobin below 13.5 g/dL, sodium below 135 mmol/L, creatinine above 1.6 mg/dL (141 µmol/L), glucose above 180 mg/dL (10 mmol/L); 8 or more suggests necrotising infection, but sensitivity is only 40.8% — never use it to rule out (WSES/SIS-E 2018, Section LRINEC).
Imaging must not delay surgery (grade 1A); plain X-ray cannot rule out (grade 1B) (WSES/SIS-E 2018, Section Imaging).

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Drives resuscitation; does not delay theatre.

clinicalManagement.title: Call surgeons and resuscitate
actions: Call urology or general surgery, anaesthesia and critical care at once; management is multidisciplinary (WSES/SIS-E 2018, grade 1C).
Contact and droplet precautions for 24 hours after the first broad-spectrum dose (VUMC protocol).

clinicalManagement.title: Start antibiotics
actions: Broad empirical cover: anti-MRSA agent plus piperacillin-tazobactam, a carbapenem, or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole (IDSA 2014, Recommendation VIII.2) — see Medicines.
Add clindamycin for suspected streptococcal or clostridial toxin disease (IDSA 2014, Section VIII).

clinicalManagement.title: Source control
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as possible and within 12 hours
actions: Surgical debridement within 12 hours of admission (WSES/SIS-E 2018, grade 1B); delay beyond 12 hours raised mortality (WSES/SIS-E 2018, Section Source control).
Do not wait for imaging (WSES/SIS-E 2018, grade 1A).

clinicalManagement.title: Re-look surgery
actions: Return to theatre 24–36 hours after the first debridement and daily until no more is needed (IDSA 2014, Section VIII).
Faecal management system or diverting colostomy per surgeon; colostomy has not reduced mortality (StatPearls, Section Treatment / Management).

clinicalManagement.title: Control glucose
actions: Target glucose 6.1–8.3 mmol/L (110–150 mg/dL); insulin if above 8.3 mmol/L (150 mg/dL) (VUMC protocol).
Insulin infusion in the intensive care unit (ICU) if two readings above 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) (VUMC protocol).

clinicalManagement.title: Narrow and stop
actions: Group A streptococcus: penicillin plus clindamycin (IDSA 2014, Recommendation VIII.3).
Stop when no further debridement is needed, improved and afebrile 48–72 hours (IDSA 2014, Section VIII).

regimens.indication: Empirical broad Gram-negative and anaerobic cover
regimens.dose: 3.375 g every 6 hours, or 4.5 g every 8 hours
regimens.duration: Until no further debridement is needed, clinically improved and afebrile 48–72 hours (IDSA 2014, Section VIII)
adjustments: IDSA 2014 lists piperacillin-tazobactam, a carbapenem, or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole as the partner to an anti-MRSA agent.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so Saudi registration was not verified; check the register and the hospital formulary before prescribing.
Paediatric: Adult-only topic — use the paediatric surgical pathway.

Penicillin allergy: Contraindicated in penicillin allergy. Alternative: Immediate or severe penicillin allergy: linezolid plus meropenem, or cefepime with metronidazole (VUMC protocol); IDSA also lists a fluoroquinolone plus metronidazole with an anti-MRSA agent — microbiology advice.

CKD: creatinine clearance 20–40 mL/min: 2.25 g every 6 h (3.375 g every 6 h for nosocomial pneumonia); below 20 mL/min: 2.25 g every 8 h (2.25 g every 6 h for nosocomial pneumonia); haemodialysis: 2.25 g every 12 h plus 0.75 g after each session (product label). [batch-01 renal/hepatic table; label not re-opened in this task]
CLD: No dose change. [batch-01 renal/hepatic table; label not re-opened in this task]
monitoring: Renal function, full blood count and lactate daily while critically ill.
Operative findings and cultures at each debridement.

medicationPlan.note: Antibiotics never replace surgery within 12 hours. Give both rows of the chosen branch together (different classes, different purposes); add the clindamycin branch only when streptococcal or clostridial toxin disease is suspected. Doses are from a review; confirm with the hospital protocol. Paediatric, penicillin-allergy, chronic kidney disease (CKD) and chronic liver disease (CLD) lines on every row. SFDA registration not verified.

learningObjectives: Get the patient to theatre within 12 hours.
keyPoints: Pain out of proportion is the early sign.
A low LRINEC never rules out.
pitfalls: Treating as cellulitis or abscess and discharging.
Waiting for CT before calling surgeons.
Stopping antibiotics before debridement is complete.

patientEducation: Explain that several operations are usually needed and why.
After discharge, report fever, new pain or wound change at once.
lifestyleAndDiet: Keep glucose controlled after discharge with the diabetes team.
Reduce alcohol; it is a common risk factor (StatPearls, Section Etiology).
dischargeCriteria: Debridement complete, sepsis resolved, wound plan and glucose plan in place.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Surgical wound and reconstruction follow-up; diabetes review; HbA1c above 7 is linked to worse outcome (StatPearls, Section Prognosis).
